title: Bring My Cup! Personalizing Vision-Language-Action Models with Visual Attentive Prompting
claim: Generic models can't act on user-specific instances; grounding the instance from a memory and prompting visually enables it without training.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, block arrows; reference images then grounding then execution
description: A left-to-right strip of three stages joined by large block arrows. At left, a column of five photos of an orange shiba-dog mug from different angles, labeled '5 images of <my cup>' (green highlighted token). The middle panel is a real photo of a robot arm facing a shelf of similar cups. A cartoon user says 'Hey robot, bring <my cup>', and a robot icon replies that according to the memory <my cup> is the shiba mug. Cups are outlined by colored segmentation masks, and the correct one is highlighted bright green, with a 'Grounding <my cup>' label. The right panel shows the robot gripper reaching the green-outlined mug, with the robot saying 'Here is <my cup>!' and the user saying 'Thanks!'. The eye goes first to the green-highlighted mug.
caption: Manipulating personal objects with VLA. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models cannot handle personal objects such as <my cup>, because they can only interpret generic, language-expressible semantics. We address this limitation with a simple framework, \lname (\Ours). It first grounds the user-specific object in the scene by matching it against the memory and then uses visual prompting to guide the VLA. This pipeline enables existing VLA models to manipulate personal objects without any additional training.
abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize well to generic instructions, they struggle with personalized commands such as "bring my cup," where the robot must act on one specific instance among visually similar objects. We study this setting of manipulating personal objects, in which a VLA must identify and control a user-specific object unseen during training using only a few reference images. To address this challenge, we propose Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP), a simple-yet-effective training-free perceptual adapter that equips frozen VLAs with top-down selective attention. VAP treats the reference images as a non-parametric visual memory, grounds the personal object in the scene through open-vocabulary detection and embedding-based matching, and then injects this grounding as a visual prompt by highlighting the object and rewriting the instruction. We construct two simulation benchmarks, Personalized-SIMPLER and Personalized-VLABench, and a real-world tabletop benchmark to evaluate personalized manipulation across multiple robots and tasks. Experiments show that VAP consistently outperforms generic policies and token-learning baselines in both success rate and correct-object manipulation, helping to bridge the gap between semantic understanding and instance-level control.
